intent: Behavior-preserving simplification of the 'same arguments' check in OverlappingFieldsCanBeMergedRule. The per-argument sameArguments/stringifyValue comparison is replaced by stringifyArguments, which wraps a field's arguments in a synthetic ObjectValueNode, sorts it with sortValueNode, prints it, and compares the strings.

findings.title: Every same-name field pair now prints arguments, even with none
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the cheap pre-check before stringifying, e.g. in findConflict: `const args1 = node1.arguments ?? []; const args2 = node2.arguments ?? []; if (args1.length !== args2.length || (args1.length > 0 && stringifyArguments(args1) !== stringifyArguments(args2))) { ...differing arguments... }`, with stringifyArguments taking the argument list. Fields without arguments then skip the allocation, sort, and print() visitor pass. A differing length always implies differing printed output, so the result is unchanged.
findings.why_it_matters: Queries that select the same field in several places, such as `id` or `name` repeated across fragments, now validate noticeably slower. Before, two argument-less fields were compared with a length check that returned immediately. Now every compared pair builds two synthetic ObjectValueNodes, sorts them, and runs print() (a full visitor traversal) on both, even when both sides are `{}`. This rule is already the most expensive validation rule and does pairwise comparisons. On the same document with only this rule enabled, a five-fragment query went from about 265us to 430us per validate and a query with 30 repeated selections went from about 1.5ms to 20ms. A length guard before stringifying restores the old fast path without changing results.

findings.title: Duplicated-argument conflict results flip in both directions
findings.suggested_fix: Accept the new behavior, which is more correct, and pin it with a test such as `{ f(a: 1, a: 1) f(a: 1, b: 1) }` reporting differing arguments. The commit is titled as a simplification, so also note the behavior change in the changelog.
findings.why_it_matters: The commit is titled as a simplification, but conflict results change for fields with duplicated argument names. `{ f(a: 1, a: 1) f(a: 1, b: 1) }` used to pass this rule and is now reported as differing arguments. `{ f(a: 1, a: 2) f(a: 1, a: 2) }` used to be reported and now passes. The old code did a first-match `find` by name, and the new code compares the whole sorted printout. Both new results are more correct. UniqueArgumentNamesRule rejects these documents under specifiedRules, so the change is visible only to callers that run this rule alone or in a custom rule set. No test pins either behavior.
evidence: base sameArguments: `const argument2 = arguments2.find((argument) => argument.name.value === argument1.name.value);` always matches the first duplicate
adversarial scratch reproduction: `f(a: 1, a: 1)` vs `f(a: 1, b: 1)`: old conflict=false, new conflict=true; `f(a: 1, a: 2)` vs `f(a: 1, a: 2)`: old conflict=true, new conflict=false

residual_risks: (adversarial) Argument order-insensitivity now depends on naturalCompare at the top level. naturalCompare accumulates digit runs in a double, so distinct names whose numeric suffixes differ only above 2^53 (e.g. a9007199254740993 vs a9007199254740992) compare equal. The stable sort then keeps source order, and reordered arguments are falsely reported as conflicting. This is contrived and needs schema-defined argument names with 16+ digit suffixes. The comparator weakness already existed for nested input-object fields; this diff extends it to argument names.

The equivalence of the old and new comparison for ordinary (non-duplicated) arguments was spot-checked (reordering, missing args, differing counts, nested objects/lists via the existing suite), not exhaustively fuzzed.
testing_gaps: No test covers duplicated arguments on overlapping fields (e.g. `{ f(a: 1, a: 1) f(a: 1, b: 1) }`), so the behavior change in finding #2 is invisible to CI.

No performance guard or benchmark covers overlap-heavy documents. The existing validateGQL benchmark uses the introspection query, which has no same-name field pairs, so the slowdown in finding #1 would not show up there.
